items.explanation: These philosophical works by Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan appeared in the following chronological sequence: *The Heart of Hindustan* (A, 1932), *Eastern Religions and Western Thought* (C, 1939), *The Dhammapada* (D, 1950), *The Principal Upanishads* (E, 1953), and *Occasional Speeches and Writings* (B, 1956).

items.title: Q3 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The term “Trace”, which refers to the trace of the other, has been borrowed by Jacques Lacan from:
items.explanation: Jacques Lacan borrowed the concept of the 'trace of the other' from the philosopher Emmanuel Levinas, who formulated the notion in his ethical writings and phenomenology. Lacan explicitly engages with Levinas's formulation of the Other in Seminar XI (*The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis*).

items.title: Q4 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Who made the following remark?
“The Sanskrit language, whatever be its antiquity, is of a wonderful structure; more perfect than the Greek, more copious than the Latin, and more exquisitely refined than either, yet bearing to both of them a stronger affinity, both in the roots of verbs and in the forms of grammar, than could possibly have been produced by accident.”
items.explanation: Sir William Jones delivered this famous address on February 2, 1786, during his Third Anniversary Discourse to the Asiatic Society of Bengal in Calcutta. His observation that Sanskrit shares an intricate grammatical and structural affinity with Greek and Latin founded modern comparative philology and established the Indo-European language family.

items.title: Q9 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods and Materials in English
items.stem: Which of the following is not a kind of literary research?
items.explanation: Experimental research relies on laboratory trials, empirical testing, and manipulation of physical variables, which belong to the empirical sciences rather than literary scholarship. Literary research employs qualitative, historical, and textual methodologies such as bibliography, biography, and interpretive analysis.

items.title: Q10 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Read the following statements carefully and choose the correct ones:
A. Patrick White, Christina Stead and Robertson Davies are the famous Australian novelists.
B. The notion of “civilized barbarity” was anticipated in H. Rider Haggard’s 1887 novel Allan Quatermain, in which “Civilization” is said to be “only savagery silver-gilt”.
C. Novels like French Lieutenant’s Woman, Midnight’s Children and Waterland deconstruct traditional notions of history and subjectivity.
D. O’Brian’s Country Girls trilogy and McGahern’s The Dark which were banned in Ireland were published during 1950s.
E. The trauma of the mid-century years accounts for the prevalence of dystopian elements in novels like A Clockwork Orange, Lanark and The Handmaid’s Tale.
items.explanation: Statements B, C, and E are correct: H. Rider Haggard's *Allan Quatermain* (1887) describes civilization as 'savagery silver-gilt', postmodern historiographic metafiction deconstructs historical narratives, and mid-century trauma inspired dystopian works like *Lanark* and *The Handmaid's Tale*. Statement A is false because Robertson Davies is Canadian rather than Australian, and statement D is false because Edna O'Brien's *The Country Girls* (1960) and John McGahern's *The Dark* (1965) appeared in the 1960s, not the 1950s.

items.title: Q11 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Erziehungsroman is a term which signifies:
items.explanation: *Erziehungsroman* is a German literary term meaning 'novel of education' or 'novel of upbringing', derived from *Erziehung* (education or training). It describes a narrative centered on the pedagogical, moral, and intellectual development of a protagonist, functioning as a specialized category of the Bildungsroman.

items.title: Q12 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Choose the correct statements regarding scope of linguistics from the following:
A. To describe and trace the history of all observable languages.
B. To determine the forces that are permanently and universally at work in all languages.
C. To study manifestations of civilized human speech only.
D. To consider only correct speech and flowery language.
E. To delimit and define itself.
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and E are the three fundamental tasks of linguistics explicitly defined by Ferdinand de Saussure in his *Course in General Linguistics* (1916). Statements C and D are false because modern linguistics is descriptive and universal, studying all manifestations of human speech without restricting itself to 'civilized' or 'flowery' language.

options: give representation to Indians in policy making.

items.explanation: Lord Curzon used the findings of the 1902 Indian Universities Commission to exert strict governmental supervision and centralize colonial education. This policy led directly to the establishment of the central office of Director-General of Education to oversee schooling standards across British India.

items.explanation: Mikhail Bakhtin introduced the literary concept of the 'chronotope' (literally 'time-space') in his 1937–38 essay 'Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel'. It refers to the intrinsic interconnectedness of temporal and spatial indicators in literary narrative.

items.explanation: In developmental linguistics, the chronological schedule of first language acquisition proceeds as: Cooing (D, ~2–4 months), Babbling (E, ~6–10 months), the One-Word/Holophrastic stage (C, ~12–18 months), the Two-Word stage (A, ~18–24 months), and Telegraphic Speech (B, ~24+ months).

items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Choose the statements given by Virginia Woolf about women:
A. “She is born stupid and can do nothing but stupidity.”
B. “She dominates the lives of kings and conquerors in fiction.”
C. “She pervades poetry from cover to cover; she is all but absent from history.”
D. She criticized Shakespeare for being harsh and rude to his female characters in his plays.
E. “(I)n real life she could hardly read, could scarcely spell, and was the property of her husband”.
items.explanation: Statements B, C, and E are direct quotations from Chapter 3 of Virginia Woolf's *A Room of One's Own* (1929), contrasting women's heroic prominence in fictional poetry with their absolute legal subjugation and erasure from historical records. Statements A and D are inaccurate caricatures never written by Woolf.

items.title: Q18 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Choose the correct statements.
A. English literature was first offered as a subject of study at King’s College, London in 1831.
B. English was first offered as a subject of study in England only in 1828 in the universities of Oxford and Cambridge.
C. Though taught as a medium of instruction and a subject of study in India since 1850s, Oxford and Cambridge did not allow the new subject of English literature to be taught till the end of the nineteenth century.
D. In 1931, English replaced the study of classics in Greek and Latin (the language of the Church) in Oxford and Cambridge.
E. Till the end of the nineteenth century literature meant only the study of great books in classical languages like Greek and Latin in Oxford and Cambridge.
items.explanation: Statements A, C, and E are historically accurate: King's College London introduced English literature as an academic subject in 1831, whereas Oxford and Cambridge resisted English studies until the end of the nineteenth century, restricting literary education strictly to classical Greek and Latin. Statements B and D are factually untrue regarding the curricular history of Oxbridge.

B. Visit your own university library

items.explanation: In *The Handbook to Literary Research*, Delia da Sousa Correa and W. R. items.title: Q20 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Which of the following statements have been given by Barbara Johnson:
A. “Deconstruction is not synonymous with destruction…”
B. “The deconstruction of a text does not proceed by random doubt or arbitrary subversion…”
C. “Deconstruction is not a dismantling of the structure of a text but a demonstration that it has already dismantled itself.”
D. “If anything is destroyed in a deconstructive reading, it is not the text, but the claim to unequivocal domination of one mode of signifying over another.”
E: “Deconstruction as a mode of interpretation works by a careful and circumspect entering of each textual labyrinth…”
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and D are direct quotations from Barbara Johnson's introduction to *The Critical Difference* (1980), where she clarifies that deconstruction does not mean destruction but a rigorous interrogation of a text's claim to unequivocal signification. Statements C and E are formulations attributed to other deconstructive theorists.

items.title: Q23 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution and Futures
items.stem:
Choose the correct statements amongst the following:
A. Macaulay was the practical man of affairs, helping and rejoicing in the progress of his beloved country.
B. Ruskin was like a Hebrew prophet just in from the desert, and the burden of his message was, “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion!”
C. Arnold was much like the cultivated Greek; his voice was soft, his speech suave, but he left the impression that you must be deficient in culture.
D. Newman was like the best French prose writers in expressing his thought with such naturalness and apparent ease that, without thinking of style, we received exactly the impression which he meant to convey.
items.explanation: Statements A, C, and D are authentic literary characterizations of Thomas Babington Macaulay, Matthew Arnold, and Cardinal John Henry Newman from William J. Long's *English Literature*. Statement B is incorrect because Long applied the comparison of a 'Hebrew prophet just in from the desert' shouting 'Woe to them that are at ease in Zion!' to Thomas Carlyle, not John Ruskin.

items.explanation: Charles Grant, a director of the British East India Company, drafted the first blueprint on English education in India in 1792 titled *Observations on the State of Society among the Asiatic Subjects of Great Britain*, advocating the introduction of Western literature and the English language.

items.stem: The study of how human beings acquire language and how we use language to speak and understand is called:
items.explanation: Psycholinguistics is the branch of cognitive science and linguistics that studies how human beings psychologically acquire, produce, comprehend, and mentally process spoken and written language.

items.title: Q26 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who has described his criticism as a “by-product” of his “private poetry-workshop” and as “a prolongation of the thinking that went into the formation of my own verse”?
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot described his critical writing in his 1956 lecture 'The Frontiers of Criticism' (published in *On Poetry and Poets*, 1957) as a 'by-product' of his 'private poetry-workshop', explaining that his literary essays were extensions of the practical problems he encountered in writing verse.

items.title: Q30 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Choose the correct definitions of language:
A. Language uses symbols that are primarily vocal but may also be visual and its subfields are phonetics, phonology, writing systems, orthography, and nonverbal communication.
B. Language is used for communication and its subfields are sentence processing, pragmatics, discourse analysis, and conversation analysis.
C. Language uses symbols that have unconventionalized meanings and its subfields are universal grammar, innateness, emergentism, neurolinguistics and cross-cultural analysis.
D. Language is a systematic means of communicating ideas or feelings by the use of conventionalized signs, sounds, gestures, or marks having understood meanings.
E. Language has region specific characteristics and its subfields are phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, discourse analysis, and lexical analysis.
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and D are standard linguistic definitions of language as a vocal, visual, and conventionalized symbolic system for human communication. Statement C is incorrect because linguistic symbols rely on conventionalized, socially agreed-upon meanings to facilitate comprehension.

items.title: Q31 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose

Which of the following critics are associated with Frankfurt School of German Intellectuals:
A. Walter Benjamin
B. Luara Mulvey
C. Travis Henderson
D. Max Horkheimer
E. Leo Lowenthal
items.explanation: Max Horkheimer, Walter Benjamin, and Leo Löwenthal were prominent theorists of the Frankfurt School's Institute for Social Research, pioneering Critical Theory and cultural critiques of mass society. Laura Mulvey is a contemporary feminist film theorist, and Travis Henderson is the protagonist in Wim Wenders's film *Paris, Texas*.

A. et sq.
B. idem
C. loc. cit.
D. passim
(Meaning)
I. the same
II. in the place cited
III. everywhere
IV. and the following
items.explanation: These Latin citation abbreviations used in academic research translate as: *et sq.* (*et sequentes*) means 'and the following' (A-IV), *idem* means 'the same' (B-I), *loc. cit.* (*loco citato*) means 'in the place cited' (C-II), and *passim* means 'everywhere' or throughout the work (D-III).

items.title: Q33 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Choose the correct key points related to approach to Feminism and Gender Studies:
A. Feminism is concerned with the marginalization of women in a patriarchal culture.
B. Feminist critics explain how the subordination of women is reflected or challenged by literary texts. They examine the experiences of women of all races, classes, sexual preferences, and cultures.
C. Mary Wollstonecraft defines four models of sexual difference: biological, linguistic, psychoanalytic, and cultural.
D. Feminist critics’ goals: to expose patriarchal premises and resulting prejudices, to promote the discovery and reevaluation of literature by women, and to examine social, cultural, and psychosexual contexts of literature and literary criticism.
E. Simone de Beauvoir prefers “womanism” to “feminism.”
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and D accurately describe the core tenets and goals of feminist literary theory and gender studies. Statement C is false because Elaine Showalter—not Mary Wollstonecraft—formulated the four models of difference in 'Feminist Criticism in the Wilderness' (1981), and statement E is false because Alice Walker coined and championed 'womanism'.

Saussurean linguistics focuses on abstract language structure (*langue*) rather than contextual, socially situated discourse (*parole*).

II. A term for the contrast between positive and negative in sentences, clauses, and phrases
III. A habitual association between particular words
IV. A term in which a word takes various forms to show its grammatical role
items.explanation: These linguistic concepts match their descriptions: 'Collocation' denotes habitual lexical co-occurrence (A-III), 'Inflected' refers to words taking variable forms to indicate grammatical roles (B-IV), 'Polarity' marks the grammatical contrast between affirmative and negative constructions (C-II), and 'Generative' refers to Noam Chomsky's formal, rule-governed linguistic model (D-I).

items.explanation: These classic works match their authors: Dadabhai Naoroji authored the landmark economic critique *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (A-II, 1901), Romesh Chunder Dutt translated his historical romance *The Slave Girl of Agra* (B-I, 1909), Manmohan Ghose published *Love Songs and Elegies* (C-IV, 1898), and Rabindranath Tagore wrote the novel *Gora* (D-III, 1909).

items.title: Q38 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Pidgin
B. Creole
C. Idiolect
D. Register
I. The language special to an individual, sometimes described as a ‘personal dialect’.
II. A language defined according to social use, such as scientific, formal, religious, and journalistic.
III. A contact language which draws on elements from two or more languages
IV. A term relating to people and languages especially in the erstwhile colonial tropics and subtropics, in the Americas, Africa, the Indian Ocean, and Oceania.
items.explanation: These sociolinguistic terms match their definitions: a pidgin is a contact language drawing on two or more languages without native speakers (A-III), creole designates contact languages nativized in colonial plantation regions (B-IV), an idiolect is an individual's unique personal speech variety (C-I), and a register is a variety determined by social and functional domain (D-II).

items.title: Q39 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Who among the following is considered as “the father of South African English poetry”?
items.explanation: Thomas Pringle (1789–1834), a Scottish poet, abolitionist, and editor who emigrated to South Africa in 1820, is regarded as the father of South African English poetry for works such as *Ephemerides* (1828) and *African Sketches* (1834).

items.title: Q40 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Kipling’s story “Mrs Bathurst” is set in
items.explanation: Rudyard Kipling's enigmatic modernist short story 'Mrs Bathurst' (collected in *Traffics and Discoveries*, 1904) is set in South Africa, taking place at a railway siding near Simon's Town on the Cape Peninsula.

items.title: Q41 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The term “Remainder” has been first used by-
items.explanation: Jacques Derrida developed the concept of the 'remainder' (*le reste*) in works such as *Limited Inc* and *Glas* to theorize that which resists, exceeds, or survives outside totalizing structural and conceptual systems.

items.title: Q42 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Choose the correct statements.
A. Miller’s play The Crucible was first written in verse.
B. The American Dream is a play by Edward Albee about the absurd situation and immediate realities.
C. The American Dream is a novel by lonesco about the problems of a middle aged professional.
D. Miller’s play The Price is set in a baroque palace in eastern Europe teasing social and metaphysical sophistication that debates not only the responsibility of the writer but the extent to which reality is composed of a series of performed gestures.
E. Miller’s play The Price explores the extent to which we retrospectively invent our own history.
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and E are correct: Arthur Miller initially attempted *The Crucible* in blank verse, Edward Albee's *The American Dream* (1961) is a seminal absurdist play, and Miller's *The Price* (1968) dramatizes how estranged brothers retrospectively reconstruct their family past. Statement C is false because *The American Dream* is not by Ionesco, and statement D is false because *The Price* is set in a Manhattan brownstone attic, not an Eastern European palace.

items.title: Q43 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Since the publication of Samuel Johnson’s “Preface to Shakespeare” in 1765, which of the Unities have been regarded as optional devices, available as needed by playwrights in England to achieve special effects of dramatic concentration?
items.explanation: In his 1765 *Preface to Shakespeare*, Samuel Johnson rejected neoclassical dogma by demonstrating that the unities of time and place are optional conventions rather than dramatic necessities, arguing that spectators are never deceived into thinking the stage is reality and leaving only the unity of action as essential.

items.title: Q44 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Identify the correct chronological order as per the publication years of the following works:
A. Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions and Times
B. The Advancement of Learning
C. Inquiry into the Original of our Idea of Beauty and Virtues
D. The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
items.explanation: The chronological sequence of these philosophical and literary works by publication year is: Francis Bacon's *The Advancement of Learning* (B, 1605), Lord Shaftesbury's *Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions and Times* (A, 1711), Francis Hutcheson's *Inquiry into the Original of our Idea of Beauty and Virtues* (C, 1725), and Samuel Johnson's *The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language* (D, 1747).

items.title: Q45 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following works is written by Joseph Conrad?
options: The Madonna of the Future and other Tales
items.explanation: *Tales of Unrest* (1898) is a short-story collection by Joseph Conrad containing 'Karain: A Memory', 'The Idiots', 'An Outpost of Progress', 'The Return', and 'The Lagoon'. The other three titles (*The Madonna of the Future*, *The Two Magics*, and *The Spoils of Poynton*) were written by Henry James.

items.title: Q46 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Identify the subtitle of Oliver Goldsmith’s semi-autobiographical poem, “The Traveller:
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith published his philosophical and semi-autobiographical poem in December 1764 with the full title *The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society*, analyzing social conditions and human happiness across Europe.

items.title: Q47 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods and Materials in English
items.stem:
Which of the following rules are correct regarding formatting of date and time in the body of thesis writing according to MLA Handbook 9th Edition?
A. When using the month-day-year style in prose, a comma must be placed after the year unless another punctuation mark follows it.
B. Use a comma between month and year or between season and year.
C. Decades can be written out or expressed in numerals.
D. Spell out centuries in uppercase letters.
E. Numerals are used for most times of the day. Generally, use the twelve hour-clock system in prose.
items.explanation: In the MLA Handbook (9th edition), rules A, C, and E are correct: month-day-year style requires a comma after the year in running text, decades may be spelled out or written with numerals, and standard twelve-hour numerals are used for times. Rule B is false because no comma separates month or season from the year, and rule D is false because centuries should be spelled out in lowercase letters.

items.title: Q48 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: In how many volumes George Eliot’s Middlemarch was first published?
items.explanation: George Eliot's *Middlemarch, A Study of Provincial Life* was first published by William Blackwood in eight separate bimonthly paperback parts (volumes) between December 1871 and December 1872.

items.title: Q49 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Feminism in chronological order:
A. The Female Imagination
B. The Madwoman in the Attic
C. A Literature of their Own
D. Women’s Oppression Today: Problems in Marxist Feminist Analysis
E. Revolution in Poetic Language
items.explanation: These landmark feminist critical works appeared chronologically as: Julia Kristeva's *Revolution in Poetic Language* (E, 1974), Patricia Meyer Spacks's *The Female Imagination* (A, 1975), Elaine Showalter's *A Literature of their Own* (C, 1977), Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar's *The Madwoman in the Attic* (B, 1979), and Michèle Barrett's *Women's Oppression Today* (D, 1980).

items.title: Q50 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Which of the Schools of Criticism has strongly opposed Formalism, in both its European and American Varieties, rejecting the view that there is a sharp and definable division between ordinary language and literary language:
A. Marxism
B. Reader Response Criticism
C. Speech —Act Theory
D. New Historicism
E. Postcolonialism
items.explanation: As noted in M. H. Abrams's *A Glossary of Literary Terms*, Reader-Response criticism (B), Speech-Act theory (C), and New Historicism (D) reject Formalism's rigid boundary between poetic and everyday language, approaching literary texts as communicative actions and culturally embedded discourses.

items.title: Q51 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution and Futures
items.stem: Who wrote to the Committee of Public Instruction on introducing English as official language of the Government and that of education?
items.explanation: Governor-General Lord William Bentinck officially directed the Committee of Public Instruction through the English Education Act resolution of March 7, 1835, decreeing that British government funds should be devoted exclusively to English-medium higher education.

items.title: Q52 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Name the theory which assumes that “culture is not separate from nature, and that there is no hierarchy of actants such that the human is more privileged”.
items.explanation: Actor-Network Theory (ANT), pioneered by Bruno Latour, Michel Callon, and John Law, adopts the principle of generalized symmetry, treating human and non-human actors equally as 'actants' and rejecting any foundational hierarchy between nature and culture.

items.title: Q53 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Match the column:
(Novel)

B. Sybil
C. Frankenstein
D. Oliver Twist
(Subtitle)
I. The Modern Prometheus
II. The Parish Boy’s Progress
III. The Two Nations
IV. The Weaver of Raveloe
items.explanation: These Victorian novels match their original subtitles: George Eliot's *Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe* (A-IV, 1861), Benjamin Disraeli's *Sybil; or, The Two Nations* (B-III, 1845), Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus* (C-I, 1818), and Charles Dickens's *Oliver Twist; or, The Parish Boy's Progress* (D-II, 1838).

items.title: Q54 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Who has coined the phrase “Bricolage”?
items.explanation: Claude Lévi-Strauss introduced the concept of 'bricolage' (and the figure of the 'bricoleur') in *The Savage Mind* (*La Pensée sauvage*, 1962) to describe how mythical and cultural systems are assembled using whatever symbolic fragments and resources are at hand.

items.title: Q55 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. “Liberty of the Press”
B. “The Vision of Mirza: An Oriental Allegory”
C. “On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth”
D. “Mental Slavery of Modern Workmen”
I. Thomas de Quincey
II. John Ruskin
III. John Milton
IV. Joseph Addison
items.explanation: These prose writings match their authors: John Milton argued for freedom of the press in *Areopagitica* (A-III, 1644), Joseph Addison published 'The Vision of Mirza' in *The Spectator* (B-IV, 1711), Thomas De Quincey wrote 'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth' (C-I, 1823), and John Ruskin critiqued dehumanizing industrial labor in 'The Nature of Gothic' / 'The Mental Slavery of Modern Workmen' (D-II, 1853).

items.title: Q56 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Jacques Derrida’s “Archive Fever: A Freudian Impression” is related to
items.explanation: Jacques Derrida's *Archive Fever: A Freudian Impression* (1995) directly interrogates archival research methodology, exploring how institutional preservation technologies, psychoanalytic memory, and state power shape archives.

items.title: Q57 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who among the following Mughal rulers carried out an experiment for newborn babies to be raised in silence, only to find that the children produced no speech at all?
items.explanation: Mughal Emperor Akbar conducted a language deprivation experiment by isolating newborn infants in the *Gang Mahal* (Dumb House) near Agra under the care of mute nurses; as recorded by Abul Fazl in the *Akbarnama*, the children developed no speech at all, proving that language requires social interaction.

items.title: Q58 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Criticism chronologically:
A. Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity
B. A History of Gay Literature: The Male Tradition
C. History of Sexuality
D. New Lesbian Criticism: Literary and Cultural Readings
E. Bodies That Matter
items.explanation: The chronological order of these works in gender and queer theory is: Michel Foucault's *The History of Sexuality, Vol. 1* (C, 1976), Judith Butler's *Gender Trouble* (A, 1990), Sally Munt's *New Lesbian Criticism* (D, 1992), Judith Butler's *Bodies That Matter* (E, 1993), and Gregory Woods's *A History of Gay Literature* (B, 1998).

items.title: Q59 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Choose the correct chronological order of the given works on Postcolonial Criticism:
A. In Other Worlds
B. Postcolonial Literary Studies: First Thirty Years
C. Nation and Narration
D. The Protestant Ethnic and the Spirit of Acapitalism
E. Modernity at Large: Cultural Dimensions of Globalization
items.explanation: These postcolonial and globalization texts appeared chronologically as: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's *In Other Worlds* (A, 1987), Homi K. Bhabha's edited collection *Nation and Narration* (C, 1990), Arjun Appadurai's *Modernity at Large* (E, 1996), Rey Chow's *The Protestant Ethnic and the Spirit of Asian Capitalism* (D, 2002), and *Postcolonial Literary Studies: First Thirty Years* (B, 2008).

items.title: Q60 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of John Storey in their chronological order of publication:
A. Inventing Popular Culture: From Folklore to Globalisation
B. Cultural Theory and Popular Culture: An Introduction
C. What is Cultural Studies: A Reader
D. Cultural Consumption and Everyday Life
E. Culture and Power in Cultural Studies: The Politics of Signification
items.explanation: John Storey's cultural studies works were published in the following sequence: *Cultural Theory and Popular Culture: An Introduction* (B, 1993), *What is Cultural Studies: A Reader* (C, 1996), *Cultural Consumption and Everyday Life* (D, 1999), *Inventing Popular Culture* (A, 2003), and *Culture and Power in Cultural Studies* (E, 2010).

items.title: Q61 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who, amongst the following, attempted to reconcile discrepancies between various classical authors such as Plato and Aristotle, as well as between philosophy and poetry?
items.explanation: The Neoplatonists (including Plotinus, Porphyry, and Proclus) harmonized philosophical discrepancies between Plato and Aristotle, reconciling philosophy and poetry by interpreting mythological narratives and poetic symbols as allegorical expressions of higher metaphysical truth.

items.title: Q62 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: “Territorialization” is a term given by-
items.explanation: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari introduced the concept of 'territorialization' (along with deterritorialization and reterritorialization) in *Anti-Oedipus* (1972) and *A Thousand Plateaus* (1980) to describe how social regimes, habits, and spatial borders regulate and constrain desire.

items.title: Q63 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who said that “Shakespeare was the Homer, or father of our dramatic poets; Johnson was the Vergil, the pattern of elaborate writing”?
items.explanation: John Dryden made this celebrated comparative assessment through the character of Neander in *An Essay of Dramatic Poesy* (1668), praising Shakespeare's organic, comprehensive imagination as akin to Homer's, while likening Ben Jonson's learned classical discipline to Virgil's.

items.title: Q64 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Read the following statements carefully and choose the correct ones:
A. A mixed metaphor conjoins two or more obviously diverse metaphoric vehicles.
B. In metonymy, a part of something is used to signify the whole.
C. To scan a passage of verse is to go through it line by line to analyze its content, theme and diction.
D. The term ‘kenning’ denotes the recurrent use, in the poems written in old Germanic languages, of a descriptive phrase in place of the ordinary name for something.
E. Figurative language is often divided into two categories: Tropes and Schemes.
items.explanation: Statements A, D, and E are authentic definitions from M. H. Abrams's *A Glossary of Literary Terms*. Statement B is false because using a part to represent the whole defines synecdoche rather than metonymy, and statement C is false because scansion specifically measures verse meter and rhythm rather than theme and diction.

items.title: Q65 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:

items.explanation: These landmark reader-response critical texts match their authors: Stanley Fish wrote *Surprised by Sin: The Reader in Paradise Lost* (A-II, 1967), Norman Holland authored *Five Readers Reading* (B-IV, 1975), Louise Rosenblatt published *The Reader, the Text, the Poem* (C-I, 1978), and Walter J. Slatoff wrote *With Respect to Readers* (D-III, 1970).

items.title: Q66 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who described Raja Rammohun Roy as ‘the inaugurator of the modern age in India’?
items.explanation: Rabindranath Tagore described Raja Rammohun Roy as 'the inaugurator of the modern age in India' during Roy's death centenary in 1933, honoring his pioneering role in launching the Bengal Renaissance, educational modernization, and social reform.

items.title: Q67 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Identify the set of poems written by W. B. Yeats.
options: “The Home-Coming”, “Among School Children”, “Byzantium”, “When You Are Old”
“Sailing to Byzantium”, “Leda and the Swan”, “The Second Coming”, “The House of Life””
“No Second Troy”, “Lapis Lazuli”, “Easter 1916”, “When You Are Old”
items.explanation: All four poems in option 4—'No Second Troy' (1910), 'Lapis Lazuli' (1938), 'Easter 1916' (1916), and 'When You Are Old' (1893)—were composed by W. B. Yeats. The alternative options include poems by other writers, such as Matthew Arnold's 'Sohrab and Rustum' and Dante Gabriel Rossetti's 'The House of Life'.

items.title: Q68 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who has designed “Panopticon” and used the term as “a new mode of obtaining power of mind over mind”?
items.explanation: Utilitarian philosopher Jeremy Bentham designed the Panopticon in 1787, describing its circular inspection architecture as 'a new mode of obtaining power of mind over mind, in a quantity hitherto without example'.

items.title: Q69 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which of the following works is not written by William Cooper?
items.explanation: *The Field-Marshal's Memoirs* (1975) was written by Anglo-Indian military novelist John Masters. William Cooper (pseudonym of Harry Summerfield Hoff) authored the other three novels—*Scenes from Provincial Life* (1950), *Scenes from Married Life* (1961), and *Memoirs of a New Man* (1966)—which pioneered post-war British provincial realism.

items.title: Q70 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods and Materials in English
items.stem: Which bibliography is concerned with the close analysis of individual copies of books in the light of our knowledge of how books were produced in literary research?
items.explanation: Analytical bibliography (or critical bibliography) examines the physical evidence of individual copies of printed books—including paper, watermarks, typography, and binding—to reconstruct the printing process and understand textual variants.

items.title: Q71 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: According to the 1991 census, ____ languages are considered scheduled languages.
items.explanation: At the time of the 1991 Census of India, the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution recognized 18 scheduled languages, following the 71st Constitutional Amendment in 1992 which added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali. The total expanded to 22 following the 92nd Constitutional Amendment in 2003.

items.title: Q72 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Who is of the opinion that the concept of “ideology” is “the most important conceptual category in cultural studies”?
items.explanation: Graeme Turner asserts in *British Cultural Studies: An Introduction* (1990) that 'ideology is the most important conceptual category in cultural studies,' central to analyzing how cultural texts produce social meaning and sustain power hierarchies.

items.title: Q73 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which group of the poets among the following is known as the Georgian Poets?
options: Alfred Noyce, W. B. Yeats, W. H. Davis, W. W. Gibson
Rupert Brooke, Walter de la Mare, John Drinkwater, James Elroy Flecker
John Masefield, Roy Campbell, Robert Graves, Dylan Thomas
W. B. Yeats, T. S. Eliot, Thomas Hardy, D. H. Lawrence
items.explanation: Rupert Brooke, Walter de la Mare, John Drinkwater, and James Elroy Flecker were prominent contributors to Edward Marsh's five anthologies of *Georgian Poetry* (1912–1922), which championed pastoral themes and lyricism during the reign of King George V.

items.title: Q74 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who has written, “The two pillars upon which a theory of criticism must rest are an account of value and an account of communication”?
items.explanation: I. A. Richards formulated this foundational principle in Chapter 4 of *Principles of Literary Criticism* (1924), asserting that any systematic critical theory requires a psychological theory of value and an empirical theory of communication.

items.title: Q75 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: The “notion of author’ constitutes the privileged moment of individualization in the history of ideas, knowledge, literature, philosophy, and the sciences.” Identify the critical essay in which the line occurs:
items.explanation: Michel Foucault opens his seminal 1969 essay 'What is an Author?' (*Qu'est-ce qu'un auteur?*) with this statement, exploring how the modern concept of the author serves to regulate, limit, and classify textual meaning.

items.title: Q76 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which of the following statements has been given by J.S. Mill in his The Subjection of Women:
A. “The husband was called the lord of the wife.”
B. “She is a slave of any boy whose parents forces a ring upon her finger.”
C. “Wives are in general no better treated than slaves.”
D. “The wife is the actual bondservant of her husband.”
E. “If all women are not the victim of actual rape, then all of them are the victims of the threat of rape.”
items.explanation: Statements A, C, and D are direct arguments from John Stuart Mill's *The Subjection of Women* (1869), in which he compares the legal subjugation of Victorian wives to chattel slavery and bondservice. Statements B and E are from modern feminist writers, with E originating in Susan Brownmiller's *Against Our Will* (1975).

items.title: Q77 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
For Arnold, Culture is:
A. the ability to know what is best;
B. the ability to know what is worst
C. the mental and spiritual application of what is best
D. the pursuit of what is best
E. the pursuit of what is worst
items.explanation: In *Culture and Anarchy* (1869), Matthew Arnold defines culture through statements A, C, and D as knowing the best that has been thought and said, applying that knowledge spiritually and mentally, and actively pursuing inward human perfection ('sweetness and light').

items.title: Q78 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story

Il. Lady Chatterley’s Lover
III. Sons and Lovers
IV. The Rainbow
items.explanation: These literary couples match D. H. Lawrence's major novels: Ursula Brangwen and Anton Skrebensky in *The Rainbow* (A-IV, 1915), Gudrun Brangwen and Gerald Crich in *Women in Love* (B-I, 1920), Connie Chatterley and Oliver Mellors in *Lady Chatterley's Lover* (C-II, 1928), and Paul Morel and Miriam Leivers in *Sons and Lovers* (D-III, 1913).

items.title: Q79 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following statements chronologically in order of their appearance in Aristotle’s Poetics:
A. The plot is “the end at which tragedy aims”.
B. Regarding the Plot, “A whole is what has a beginning and middle and end”.
C. The plot of the tragedy should have a Unity: “the component incidents must be so arranged that if one of them be transposed or removed, the unity of the whole is dislocated and destroyed”.
D. The character in question must occupy a mean between these extremes: he must be a man “who is not pre-eminently virtuous and just, and yet it is through no badness or villainy of his own that he falls into the misfortune, but rather through some flaw in him”.
E. The function of the poet is to narrate “events such as might occur … in accordance with the laws of probability or necessity”.
items.explanation: These statements appear sequentially across chapters of Aristotle's *Poetics*: Chapter 6 defines plot as the end and soul of tragedy (A), Chapter 7 requires a plot to have a beginning, middle, and end (B), Chapter 8 establishes organic unity (C), Chapter 9 defines poetic truth through probability or necessity (E), and Chapter 13 analyzes the tragic hero's hamartia (D).

items.title: Q80 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who has coined the term “Onto-Theology”?
items.explanation: In post-structuralist literary theory, Jacques Derrida famously utilized and popularized the term 'onto-theology' in *Of Grammatology* (1967) to critique the Western metaphysics of presence, which historically grounds meaning in an ultimate transcendent origin or deity.

items.title: Q81 · June 2025 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following statements carefully and find out the correct ones:
A. Charles Lamb was a lifelong friend of Coleridge and defender of the poetic creed of Wordsworth.
B. The London crowd, with its pleasures and occupations, never attracted Charles Lamb.
C. Charles Lamb gave us the best pen-portraits of Coleridge, Hazlitt, Landor, Hood, and many more of the interesting men and women of his age.

"From thee, even from thy virtue!
What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine?
The tempter or the tempted, who sins most?
Ha! Not she; nor doth she tempt: but it is I
That, lying by the violet in the sun,
Do as the carrion does, not as the flower,
Corrupt with virtuous season. Can it be
That modesty may more betray our sense
Than woman's lightness? Having waste ground enough,
Shall we desire to raze the sanctuary
And pitch our evils there? O, fie, fie, fie!
What dost thou, or what art thou, Angelo?
Dost thou desire her foully for those things
That make her good? O, let her brother live:
Thieves for their robbery have authority
When judges steal themselves. What, do I love her,
That I desire to hear her speak again,
And feast upon her eyes? What is't I dream on?
O cunning enemy, that, to catch a saint,
With saints dost bait thy hook!"
— William Shakespeare, Measure for Measure (Act II, Scene 2)

Question:
“Thieves for their robbery have authority / When judges steal themselves” implies what?
items.explanation: Angelo admits that judicial condemnation of petty criminals is hypocritical when the judges themselves commit moral robbery, as a corrupt magistrate possesses no ethical authority to condemn others.

items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Prose Passage]
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Painting, or art generally, as such, with all its technicalities, difficulties, and particular ends, is nothing but a noble and expressive language, invaluable as the vehicle of thought, but by itself nothing. He who has learned what is commonly considered the whole art of painting, that is, the art of representing any natural object faithfully, has as yet only learned the language by which his thoughts are to be expressed. He has done just as much toward being that which we ought to respect as a great painter, as a man, who had learned how to express himself grammatically and melodiously, would have done toward being a great poet. The language is, indeed, more difficult of acquirement in the one case than in the other, and possesses more of intrinsic beauty; but it is, nevertheless, a language only, both being capable of deep expression, but neither of them, by itself, giving any value to the conception it conveys."
— John Ruskin, Modern Painters (Volume I)

Question:
What implicit assumption about language and expression underpins the passage’s argument?
options: All forms of art must use written language to be effective.
Expression without technical skill is more valuable.
The medium of expression is secondary to the message conveyed.
The value of grammar and melody lies in their aesthetic, not communicative power
items.explanation: Ruskin argues that visual art, like verbal language, is merely a vehicle or medium of expression, meaning that technical skill is secondary to the nobility and weight of the thoughts it conveys.
